en: Time Evolution, Conservation, and Coupled Spins

p.src: Time Evolution, Conservation, and Coupled Spins

u.src: Time Evolution, Conservation, and Coupled Spins
en: Time Evolution, Conservation, and Coupled Spins

p.src: A quantum state is not a fixed point in Hilbert space. As time passes it moves, yet it must move without losing normalization, probabilities, or the distinguishability encoded in inner products. Those requirements nearly determine the form of quantum dynamics. Linearity gives a time-evolution operator, probability conservation makes that operator unitary, and an infinitesimal unitary transformation is generated by a Hermitian operator. That operator is the Hamiltonian. We shall derive the Schrödinger equation from these statements, see how energy eigenstates accumulate phase, and then turn the formalism into two concrete calculations: precession of one spin in a magnetic field and oscillation between two states of a coupled spin pair.

p.src: Linear Motion in Hilbert Space

u.src: Linear Motion in Hilbert Space
en: Linear Motion in Hilbert Space

p.src: Let the state at time $t$ be $\ket{\psi(t)}$. We assume that its relation to the state at time zero is linear: $\ket{\psi(t)}=U(t)\ket{\psi(0)}.$ The linearity is a postulate, not a theorem derived from something more elementary. It is an experimentally successful part of quantum mechanics, and attempts to replace it generally endanger either probability or conservation laws. In a chosen basis, $U(t)$ is simply a time-dependent matrix.

p.src: Probability Conservation Implies Unitarity

u.src: Probability Conservation Implies Unitarity
en: Probability Conservation Implies Unitarity

p.src: A normalized state represents total probability one: $\braket{\psi(t)}{\psi(t)}=1.$ Time evolution must preserve this norm. In fact, a linear map that preserves the norm of every vector also preserves every inner product. Geometrically, preserving the lengths of two vectors and their difference preserves the triangle formed by them and hence their angle. In a complex vector space the same conclusion follows by also considering combinations with a factor of $i$.

p.src: The Infinitesimal Generator

u.src: The Infinitesimal Generator
en: The Infinitesimal Generator

p.src: Finite evolution is built from very small time steps. Let the elapsed time be $\epsilon$, small enough that terms of order $\epsilon^2$ may be ignored. At zero elapsed time nothing happens, so $U(0)=I.$ The leading correction must be proportional to $\epsilon$. We write it in the conventional form $\boxed{U(\epsilon)=I-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H}.$ Only the factor of $\epsilon$ is forced at this stage. The $i$, $\hbar$, and the name $H$ are chosen so that the object left at the end has the standard normalization and is Hermitian.

At zero elapsed time nothing happens, so $U(0)=I.$ The leading correction must be proportional to $\epsilon$. We write it in the conventional form $\boxed{U(\epsilon)=I-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H}.$ Only the factor of $\epsilon$ is forced at this stage. p.src:
Taking the Hermitian conjugate, $U^\dagger(\epsilon)
=I+\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H^\dagger.$ Now multiply and retain only first-order terms: $\begin{aligned}
U^\dagger(\epsilon)U(\epsilon)
&=
\left(I+\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H^\dagger\right)
\left(I-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H\right) \\
&=
I+\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}\left(H^\dagger-H\right)
+O(\epsilon^2).\end{aligned}$ Unitarity requires this product to equal $I$, and therefore $\boxed{H^\dagger=H}.$ The infinitesimal generator of time evolution is Hermitian. Since Hermitian operators represent observables, every dynamical system possesses an observable that generates its motion in time. This is the Hamiltonian. We use $H$ for the operator and reserve $E$ for its possible measured values, the eigenvalues.

p.src:
A single energy eigenstate changes only by an overall phase, and an overall phase cannot affect a probability. Interesting dynamics begins when a state contains several energy eigenvectors. Since a Hermitian Hamiltonian has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, $H\ket{\psi_n}=E_n\ket{\psi_n},
\qquad
\ket{\psi(0)}=\sum_n\alpha_n\ket{\psi_n}.$

p.src: Combining Systems

u.src: Combining Systems
en: Combining Systems

p.src:
For two noninteracting systems $A$ and $B$, the combined Hamiltonian is the sum of the separate generators on the product space: $H_{AB}
=
H_A\otimes I_B+I_A\otimes H_B.$ If $H_A\ket{a}=E_a\ket{a},
\qquad
H_B\ket{b}=E_b\ket{b},$ then $H_{AB}\ket{a,b}=(E_a+E_b)\ket{a,b}.$ Energies, and therefore phase frequencies, add for separated noninteracting systems. An interaction contributes another term $H_{\mathrm{int}}$, so this simple sum no longer gives the whole energy.

p.src:
Choose the field along the third axis, $\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
H=\frac{\mu B}{2}\sigma_3.$ We shall track the expectation values of the three spin components. To shorten the equations, write $s_i(t)=\langle\sigma_i\rangle_t.$ The longitudinal component obeys $\dot s_3
=
\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle[H,\sigma_3]\rangle
=0,$ because $H$ is proportional to $\sigma_3$. The projection of the spin along the field is fixed. Geometrically, the tip of the average spin must remain on a cone of fixed opening angle about the field axis.

p.src:
For the first transverse component, $\dot s_1
=
\frac{i\mu B}{2\hbar}
\langle[\sigma_3,\sigma_1]\rangle.$ The commutator can be checked directly from $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_3&=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
&
\sigma_1&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\\[0.5em]
\sigma_2&=
\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$ Indeed, $\sigma_3\sigma_1=i\sigma_2,
\qquad
\sigma_1\sigma_3=-i\sigma_2,$ so $=2i\sigma_2.$ Consequently, $\dot s_1=-\frac{\mu B}{\hbar}s_2.$ Likewise, using $[\sigma_3,\sigma_2]=-2i\sigma_1$, $\dot s_2=\frac{\mu B}{\hbar}s_1.$

p.src: Preparation and Measurement

u.src: Preparation and Measurement
en: Preparation and Measurement

p.src: Suppose an ensemble is prepared in the $+1$ eigenstate of $\sigma_1$. At $t=0$, a measurement of $\sigma_1$ is certain to return $+1$, while measurements of $\sigma_2$ or $\sigma_3$ give equal probabilities for $\pm1$. After a quarter precession period, the state has rotated to the $+1$ eigenstate of $\sigma_2$: $\sigma_2$ is then certain and $\sigma_1$ is maximally uncertain. After another quarter period it reaches the $-1$ eigenstate of $\sigma_1$. The rotating expectation values therefore have direct operational meaning.

p.src: Triplet and Singlet Energies

u.src: Triplet and Singlet Energies
en: Triplet and Singlet Energies

p.src:
The two-spin Hilbert space has dimension four. The interaction is diagonal in the triplet–singlet basis: $\begin{aligned}
\ket{T_+}&=\ket{\uparrow\uparrow}, \\
\ket{T_0}&=
\frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}+\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}, \\
\ket{T_-}&=\ket{\downarrow\downarrow}, \\
\ket{S}&=
\frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}-\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}$ The three triplet states share one energy $E_T$; the singlet has another energy $E_S$. Thus there are four independent eigenvectors but only two distinct energy levels. The triplet level is threefold degenerate.

\frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}-\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}$ The three triplet states share one energy $E_T$; the singlet has another energy $E_S$. Thus there are four independent eigenvectors but only two distinct energy levels. The triplet level is threefold degenerate.
en:
The two-spin Hilbert space has dimension four. The interaction is diagonal in the triplet–singlet basis: $\begin{aligned}
\ket{T_+}&=\ket{\uparrow\uparrow}, \\
\ket{T_0}&=
\frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}+\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}, \\
\ket{T_-}&=\ket{\downarrow\downarrow}, \\
\ket{S}&=
\frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}-\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}$ The three triplet states share one energy $E_T$; the singlet has another energy $E_S$. Thus there are four independent eigenvectors but only two distinct energy levels. The triplet level is threefold degenerate.

p.src:
The factor $e^{-i\overline E t/\hbar}$ is common to the entire ket and drops out of every probability. The measurable probabilities are $P_{\uparrow\downarrow}(t)
=
\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\Delta E\,t}{2\hbar}\right),
\qquad
P_{\downarrow\uparrow}(t)
=
\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\Delta E\,t}{2\hbar}\right).$ The state oscillates from $\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}$ to $\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}$ and back, at a rate determined only by the energy difference. At intermediate times both amplitudes are nonzero, and except at special instants the two spins are entangled.

p.src: The calculation illustrates a general method. Choose the basis in which the physical question is posed, expand the initial state in eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian, let each eigenvector acquire its own phase, and then recombine the pieces in the measurement basis. Quantum dynamics becomes systematic once the Hamiltonian has been diagonalized; all observable motion is carried by relative phase.
